title: Hearing, Balance & the Vestibular System
summary: How we hear and stay upright, and what vertigo tells you.

lessons.title: The Cochlea & Auditory Pathway

levels.kid:
Your ear is like a tiny music machine. Sound is the air wiggling back and forth. Those wiggles go into your ear and make your eardrum shake like a drum.

Three tiny bones pass the shake along to a snail-shaped tube called the cochlea. The cochlea is full of liquid and lined with tiny hair cells. The hair cells have little bristles on top that bend when the liquid moves.

When the bristles bend, the hair cells send a message down the hearing nerve to your brain. High sounds tickle the start of the snail. Low sounds tickle the far end. Your brain puts it all together so you hear music, voices and your dog barking!
levels.hs:
Hearing turns pressure waves in air into nerve signals.

**Outer and middle ear.** Sound travels down the ear canal and vibrates the tympanic membrane (eardrum). Three ossicles, the malleus, incus and stapes, carry the vibration to the oval window of the inner ear. They act like a lever and a funnel, boosting pressure so sound is not lost moving from air into fluid.

**The cochlea.** The cochlea is a fluid-filled spiral. Running along it is the basilar membrane, which carries the organ of Corti. Its hair cells have stereocilia (tiny stiff hairs). When the membrane vibrates, stereocilia bend, ion channels open, and the hair cell releases neurotransmitter onto fibers of the cochlear nerve.

**Tonotopy.** The basilar membrane is narrow and stiff at the base and wide and floppy at the apex. High frequencies vibrate the base; low frequencies vibrate the apex. This place-to-pitch map is called tonotopy, and it is kept all the way to the cortex.

**To the brain.** The signal runs from the cochlear nerve to the cochlear nuclei in the brainstem, then the superior olive, the inferior colliculus, the medial geniculate nucleus of the thalamus and finally the primary auditory cortex in the temporal lobe. Because signals cross at several levels, each ear reaches both sides of the brain.
levels.college:
**Impedance matching.** Air-to-fluid transmission would reflect most acoustic energy. The middle ear compensates mainly through the area ratio of the tympanic membrane to the oval window (roughly 17:1) plus the ossicular lever, giving roughly a 25-30 dB gain. The stapedius (CN VII) and tensor tympani (CN V3) dampen ossicular motion; stapedius paralysis in facial palsy causes hyperacusis.

**Cochlear fluids.** The scala media contains endolymph, high in K+, with an endocochlear potential of about +80 mV generated by the stria vascularis. Scala vestibuli and tympani contain perilymph, which resembles extracellular fluid. Because the hair cell interior is negative and endolymph is positive, the driving force for K+ entry into hair cells is large, so transduction is fast and energy-efficient.

**Mechanotransduction.** Stereocilia are linked by tip links. Deflection toward the tallest stereocilium tensions tip links, opening mechanoelectrical transduction channels (TMC1/2 are core components). K+ and Ca2+ enter, the cell depolarizes, voltage-gated Ca2+ channels open, and glutamate is released at ribbon synapses.

**Inner vs outer hair cells.** About 3,500 inner hair cells provide nearly all afferent signal (type I spiral ganglion neurons). About 12,000 outer hair cells act as the cochlear amplifier: the motor protein prestin changes their length with voltage (electromotility), sharpening tuning and boosting quiet sounds. Otoacoustic emissions are a by-product used in newborn screening.

**Central pathway.** Cochlear nerve → cochlear nuclei (dorsal and ventral) → superior olivary complex (first binaural site) → lateral lemniscus → inferior colliculus → medial geniculate body → primary auditory cortex (Heschl's gyrus, Brodmann 41/42). Bilateral representation above the cochlear nuclei means a unilateral lesion above that level rarely causes one-sided deafness.
levels.phd:
**Active cochlear mechanics.** Passive basilar membrane tuning, as von Békésy described it in cadavers, is broad. Living cochleae show sharp, compressive, level-dependent tuning that disappears after death or outer hair cell loss. Prestin-driven somatic electromotility, likely working with hair-bundle active motion, injects energy cycle-by-cycle near the characteristic place, giving roughly 40-60 dB of gain at threshold and compressing a large range of sound intensity into a smaller range of membrane motion. Prestin knockout mice lose this amplification, establishing causality.

**Transduction channel biology.** Tip links are formed by cadherin-23 (upper) and protocadherin-15 (lower). Fast adaptation (Ca2+-dependent channel reclosure) and slower myosin-driven adaptation reset the operating point. Mutations in these proteins and in TMC1 cause hereditary deafness; Usher syndrome type 1 links deafness and retinitis pigmentosa through shared ciliary and adhesion proteins.

**Coding.** Frequency is encoded by place (tonotopy) and, below roughly 4 kHz, by phase locking. Intensity is coded by firing rate and recruitment of high-threshold, low-spontaneous-rate fibers. Those low-spontaneous-rate fibers are especially vulnerable to noise, explaining **cochlear synaptopathy** ("hidden hearing loss"): normal audiogram thresholds but degraded hearing in noise after ribbon synapse loss.

**Binaural computation.** The medial superior olive computes interaural time differences with microsecond precision, aided by precisely timed glycinergic inhibition rather than only the classic Jeffress delay-line model. The lateral superior olive computes interaural level differences by comparing ipsilateral excitation with contralateral inhibition relayed through the medial nucleus of the trapezoid body via the calyx of Held, one of the largest synapses in the brain.

**Cortex.** Primary auditory cortex shows tonotopic gradients, while belt and parabelt regions process spectrotemporal patterns. A ventral "what" stream supports sound identity and speech, and a dorsal "where/how" stream supports spatial hearing and sensorimotor mapping for speech.
levels.expert:
**Bedside localization.** Start by asking: conductive or sensorineural? Weber (512 Hz fork on the vertex) lateralizes to the affected ear in conductive loss and to the better ear in sensorineural loss. Rinne compares air with bone conduction; bone louder than air means a conductive problem. Then confirm with formal audiometry and tympanometry.

**Sudden sensorineural hearing loss** is an otologic urgency. A unilateral drop over hours to days needs prompt audiometry and ENT input; early corticosteroids are standard management, and delay worsens outcomes. Sudden hearing loss with vertigo plus other brainstem signs raises concern for anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA) infarction, because the labyrinthine artery usually arises from AICA.

**Asymmetric sensorineural loss** warrants MRI with gadolinium of the internal auditory canals to exclude a vestibular schwannoma (often called acoustic neuroma). Classic presentation: progressive one-sided hearing loss, tinnitus, unsteadiness; large tumors compress CN V (reduced corneal reflex), CN VII and the brainstem. Bilateral vestibular schwannomas define neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2-related schwannomatosis).

**Neurosurgical angle.** Vestibular schwannoma management is observation with serial MRI, stereotactic radiosurgery, or microsurgery through retrosigmoid, translabyrinthine (sacrifices hearing) or middle fossa approaches. The facial nerve is the critical structure; continuous facial nerve monitoring and brainstem auditory evoked potentials guide surgery. Outcomes are graded with the House-Brackmann scale.

**Central auditory lesions** are tricky: bilateral representation means unilateral cortical stroke usually spares pure-tone hearing but impairs sound localization or speech in noise. Bilateral temporal lesions can cause cortical deafness or auditory agnosia. Auditory brainstem implants bypass the cochlear nerve in NF2, while cochlear implants need an intact nerve and stimulate spiral ganglion neurons tonotopically.

keyPoints: Ossicles (malleus, incus, stapes) amplify vibration onto the oval window (impedance matching)
Hair cells transduce bending of stereocilia; endolymph is high in K+ (+80 mV endocochlear potential)
Tonotopy: high frequencies at the cochlear base, low at the apex
Inner hair cells carry the signal; outer hair cells amplify it via prestin
Pathway: cochlear nuclei → superior olive → inferior colliculus → medial geniculate → auditory cortex (Heschl's gyrus)
Weber and Rinne separate conductive from sensorineural loss; asymmetric loss needs MRI for vestibular schwannoma

examples.src: Weber lateralizes to the right ear; Rinne on the right shows bone louder than air.
examples.tr: Right conductive hearing loss (for example earwax, fluid or otosclerosis).

examples.src: Slowly worsening left hearing loss and tinnitus with a reduced left corneal reflex.
examples.tr: Think left vestibular schwannoma large enough to touch CN V; get a gadolinium MRI.

Cochlear synaptopathy with loss of low-spontaneous-rate fiber synapses
Outer hair cell hyperfunction amplifying the background noise

lessons.title: The Vestibular Apparatus

levels.kid:
Inside each ear, right next to the hearing snail, is your balance kit. It has three little loops full of liquid and two tiny sacs with "ear rocks" on top.

When you spin your head, the liquid in the loops sloshes and bends tiny hairs. That tells your brain, "We are turning!"

The ear rocks are heavier than the jelly they sit in. When you tilt your head or speed up in a car, the rocks slide a little and bend hairs too. That tells your brain which way is down.

Your brain mixes these messages with what your eyes see and what your feet feel. That's how you can walk, run and ride a bike without falling over!
levels.hs:
The vestibular system senses head movement and gravity. It sits in the inner ear, in the bony labyrinth next to the cochlea.

**Semicircular canals.** Each ear has three canals: anterior (superior), posterior and horizontal (lateral). They sit at roughly right angles, so together they cover turning in any direction. Each canal has a swelling, the ampulla, holding a jelly flap called the cupula with hair cells underneath. When the head rotates, the endolymph lags behind because of inertia, pushes the cupula and bends the hair cells. Canals detect **angular acceleration** (turning).

**Otolith organs.** The utricle and saccule contain a sheet of hair cells covered by a gel with calcium carbonate crystals called otoconia. Because the crystals are heavy, tilting or moving in a straight line shifts the gel and bends the hairs. The utricle mainly senses horizontal movement and head tilt; the saccule mainly senses vertical movement. Otoliths detect **linear acceleration and gravity**.

**Push-pull pairs.** The canals work in pairs across the two ears. Turning your head right excites the right horizontal canal and inhibits the left one. The brain reads the difference.

**Pathway.** Signals travel in the vestibular part of cranial nerve VIII to the vestibular nuclei in the brainstem, which connect to eye-movement nuclei, the spinal cord (posture), the cerebellum and the cortex.
levels.college:
**Hair cell polarity.** Each vestibular hair cell has many stereocilia and one kinocilium. Deflection toward the kinocilium depolarizes the cell and increases afferent firing; deflection away hyperpolarizes it and reduces firing. Afferents fire tonically at rest (high resting rate), so the system can signal both directions by increasing or decreasing rate.

**Canal mechanics.** The canal behaves like an overdamped pendulum (torsion-pendulum model): over the usual frequencies of natural head movement, cupular deflection is roughly proportional to head **velocity**, even though the stimulus is acceleration. In the horizontal canal, endolymph flow toward the ampulla (ampullopetal) is excitatory; in the vertical canals, flow away from the ampulla (ampullofugal) is excitatory.

**Coplanar pairs.** Left and right horizontal canals pair together; each anterior canal pairs with the opposite posterior canal (LARP: left anterior–right posterior; RALP: right anterior–left posterior). This underlies head impulse testing of individual canals.

**Otolith organs.** The utricular macula lies roughly horizontal and the saccular macula roughly vertical. A curved line called the striola divides each macula, and hair cell polarity reverses across it, so each macula encodes every direction within its plane. Otoliths cannot tell tilt from linear acceleration on their own (Einstein's equivalence principle); the brain resolves this using canal input.

**Central connections.** The vestibular nerve (superior and inferior divisions; ganglion of Scarpa) projects to the four vestibular nuclei (superior, medial, lateral and inferior) and directly to the flocculonodular lobe of the cerebellum. Outputs include the medial longitudinal fasciculus (eye movements), the lateral vestibulospinal tract (extensor tone), the medial vestibulospinal tract (neck), and the thalamus to vestibular cortical areas such as the parieto-insular vestibular cortex.

**Blood supply.** The labyrinthine artery, usually a branch of AICA, is an end artery, so occlusion can cause sudden combined vertigo and deafness.
levels.phd:
**Two afferent classes.** Vestibular afferents divide into regular and irregular fibers. Regular afferents, mostly contacting type II hair cells via bouton endings, have precise firing and encode head motion with high fidelity. Irregular afferents, often with calyx endings around type I hair cells, are more sensitive, more phasic and better at high-frequency, transient motion. The calyx synapse is unusual: besides quantal glutamate release, it transmits through non-quantal coupling via K+ accumulation and electrical effects in the narrow synaptic cleft, enabling extremely fast transmission.

**Velocity storage.** Peripheral canal signals decay with a time constant of roughly 5-7 seconds, but perceived rotation and nystagmus last longer (often 15-20 seconds) because a brainstem-cerebellar network in the vestibular nuclei and nodulus/uvula integrates and extends the signal. Velocity storage also helps reorient the rotation axis toward gravity. Nodulus lesions disrupt it, causing periodic alternating nystagmus and abnormal tilt suppression.

**Internal models.** The brain resolves the tilt-translation ambiguity by combining canal-derived rotation estimates with otolith input in an internal model, with neurons in the caudal cerebellar vermis and vestibular nuclei encoding tilt and translation separately. Vestibular-only neurons in the vestibular nuclei respond strongly to passive motion but are suppressed during active head movements, because an efference copy predicts the expected sensory consequences. This is cancellation of reafference, a recurring principle in sensorimotor neuroscience.

**Efferent system.** Brainstem efferent neurons project back to hair cells and afferents, modulating sensitivity, possibly as part of predictive gain control.

**Cortex.** There is no single primary vestibular cortex. Instead, a distributed network including the parieto-insular vestibular cortex, the temporoparietal junction and area MST integrates vestibular, visual and proprioceptive signals for self-motion perception, spatial orientation and body ownership. Disturbances here relate to room-tilt illusions and some out-of-body experiences.
levels.expert:
**History first.** Vestibular complaints are often vague. Separate true vertigo (illusion of movement) from presyncope, imbalance and nonspecific dizziness, but remember patients describe the same disorder in different words. Timing and triggers outperform the adjective: brief positional episodes, a single acute prolonged episode, recurrent spontaneous episodes, or chronic imbalance.

**Bedside vestibular exam.**
- Head impulse test: a quick small head turn while the patient fixes on your nose. A corrective catch-up saccade means a deficient VOR on the side of the turn. Video head impulse testing quantifies canal-by-canal gain.
- Dix-Hallpike and supine roll tests for positional vertigo.
- Look for spontaneous and gaze-evoked nystagmus, ideally with fixation removed (Frenzel goggles).
- Romberg, tandem gait and Fukuda stepping for vestibulospinal function.

**Bilateral vestibulopathy** causes oscillopsia during walking and unsteadiness in the dark, with relatively little vertigo. Causes include ototoxic aminoglycosides (gentamicin can destroy vestibular hair cells, often sparing hearing), bilateral Ménière disease and CANVAS (cerebellar ataxia, neuropathy, vestibular areflexia syndrome, linked to RFC1 repeat expansions).

**Superior canal dehiscence.** A thin or absent bone over the superior canal creates a "third window": sound- or pressure-induced vertigo (Tullio phenomenon), autophony and low-frequency conductive-like hearing loss with normal or enhanced bone conduction. Diagnosis uses high-resolution CT plus vestibular evoked myogenic potentials (low thresholds, large amplitudes). Surgical plugging or resurfacing through a middle fossa or transmastoid approach can cure it.

**Operative relevance.** Neurosurgeons meet the labyrinth in skull base work: the translabyrinthine approach removes it; retrosigmoid drilling of the internal auditory canal must avoid the posterior canal and vestibule to preserve hearing. Vestibular nerve section, once used for disabling unilateral Ménière vertigo, is now rare because intratympanic therapy usually suffices.

keyPoints: Three semicircular canals (anterior, posterior, horizontal) sense angular acceleration of the head
Utricle (horizontal) and saccule (vertical) otolith organs sense linear acceleration and gravity
Endolymph inertia deflects the cupula; otoconia weight deflects the otolithic membrane
Bending toward the kinocilium excites; canals work in push-pull pairs across both ears
Vestibular nerve → vestibular nuclei → MLF (eyes), vestibulospinal tracts (posture), cerebellum

examples.src: After spinning in a chair and stopping, the room seems to keep turning.
examples.tr: Endolymph keeps moving briefly after the head stops, deflecting the cupula the opposite way, so you feel rotation in the other direction.

lessons.title: The Vestibulo-Ocular Reflex

levels.kid:
Try this: hold up your thumb, look at it, and shake your head "no." Your thumb stays clear, right? Now hold your head still and wiggle your thumb fast. It gets blurry!

That's because of a super-fast trick called the eye-steadying reflex. When your head turns one way, your balance kit in your ear tells your eye muscles to turn your eyes the other way, at the same speed. So your eyes stay locked on what you are looking at.

It works faster than you can blink. It's like a camera that holds the picture steady while you run. Doctors test it by gently turning your head and watching your eyes.
levels.hs:
The vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR) keeps your vision steady while your head moves. If your head turns right at a certain speed, your eyes turn left at the same speed, so the image stays still on the retina.

**Why it matters.** Without the VOR, every step would make the world bounce. People who lose it describe oscillopsia: the world jumping around while they walk.

**The three-neuron arc (horizontal VOR, head turning right).**
- The right horizontal canal is excited and sends more signals along the vestibular nerve.
- The right vestibular nuclei excite the opposite (left) abducens nucleus (CN VI), which moves the left eye outward (left).
- Abducens interneurons cross back and travel up the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) to the right oculomotor nucleus (CN III), which contracts the right medial rectus so the right eye also moves left.
Both eyes turn left, opposite to the head.

**Speed.** The VOR has a delay of under about 10 milliseconds, far faster than visual tracking, which is why it handles quick head movements best.

**Testing it.**
- The doll's eyes maneuver (oculocephalic reflex) in an unconscious patient: turning the head makes the eyes move the opposite way if the brainstem is working.
- Cold water in the ear (caloric testing) stimulates the canal artificially.
- The head impulse test checks each side in an awake patient.
levels.college:
**Gain and phase.** VOR gain is eye velocity divided by head velocity; ideally close to 1 for distant targets, with eye movement in the opposite direction (180° out of phase with the head). Near targets need a higher gain because the eyes are offset from the axis of rotation, and the brain adjusts for vergence.

**Neural integrator.** Canal afferents carry head velocity, but holding the eye in a new position needs a position command. Brainstem integrators convert velocity into position: the nucleus prepositus hypoglossi and medial vestibular nucleus for horizontal gaze, and the interstitial nucleus of Cajal for vertical/torsional gaze. A leaky integrator causes gaze-evoked nystagmus.

**Nystagmus.** With sustained rotation, the eyes drift slowly opposite the head (slow phase, vestibular) and then reset with a quick phase in the direction of rotation (generated by saccade circuits in the paramedian pontine reticular formation). Nystagmus is named by the fast phase.

**Caloric testing (COWS).** Cold water in the right ear cools endolymph, making it sink and flow away from the ampulla of the (vertically oriented, with head up 30°) horizontal canal: inhibition. The eyes drift slowly toward the cold ear, and the fast phase beats away: Cold Opposite, Warm Same. In a comatose patient with an intact brainstem but no cortical correction, cold water gives tonic deviation toward the irrigated ear without fast phases. No eye movement suggests severe brainstem dysfunction (a component of brain death testing).

**Head impulse test.** In a unilateral peripheral loss (for example vestibular neuritis), a rapid head turn toward the bad side produces eyes that move with the head, followed by a corrective catch-up saccade back to target. Ewald's second law explains why: excitation drives a stronger response than inhibition, so the intact side cannot fully compensate for high-speed turns toward the lesioned side.

**Adaptation.** The cerebellar flocculus adjusts VOR gain when vision and head motion mismatch, such as when wearing new magnifying glasses.
levels.phd:
**Cerebellar motor learning.** The VOR is a classic model of supervised learning. Retinal slip (image motion during head movement) is an error signal carried by climbing fibers from the inferior olive (via accessory optic system pathways) to floccular Purkinje cells. Mossy fibers carry vestibular and eye-movement signals. Pairing produces long-term depression at parallel fiber–Purkinje cell synapses, changing floccular output to the vestibular nuclei. The Marr-Albus-Ito framework predicted this; later work showed that learning also transfers to sites in the vestibular nuclei (flocculus target neurons), consistent with a two-site model in which the cortex learns quickly and the brainstem stores long-term memory. Gain-increase and gain-decrease learning use partly different mechanisms and differ in frequency generalization.

**Velocity storage and the angular VOR.** The low-frequency VOR is extended by velocity storage, which also reorients rotation estimates toward gravity during tilted rotation. Nodulus and uvula lesions abolish this tilt dumping and can produce periodic alternating nystagmus, which responds to GABA-B agonists, consistent with Purkinje inhibitory control of the storage mechanism.

**Translational VOR.** Otolith-driven eye movements compensate for linear head translation. Unlike the angular VOR, required eye velocity depends on target distance, so the translational VOR scales with vergence, showing that it is not a fixed reflex but a context-dependent computation. Ocular counter-roll during head tilt is a small otolith-driven torsional response.

**Three-dimensional geometry.** Each canal pair connects primarily to an extraocular muscle pair in a nearly matching plane: horizontal canals to medial and lateral recti; anterior canals to the ipsilateral superior rectus and contralateral inferior oblique; posterior canals to the ipsilateral superior oblique and contralateral inferior rectus. This matching underlies the characteristic nystagmus of each canal's BPPV (for example, upbeating torsional nystagmus in posterior canal BPPV).

**Compensation.** After unilateral loss, static symptoms resolve over days as commissural and cerebellar mechanisms rebalance the vestibular nuclei, while dynamic deficits at high acceleration persist, which is why head impulses stay abnormal.
levels.expert:
**The VOR in the comatose patient.** The oculocephalic and oculovestibular reflexes test the brainstem from the vestibular nuclei (medulla/pons) through the MLF to the CN III nuclei (midbrain), covering much of the brainstem's length. Before doll's eyes, clear the cervical spine; in trauma, use caloric testing instead. Check the tympanic membrane for perforation before irrigating. In formal brain death determination, absent oculovestibular responses are one required finding, interpreted only after confounders such as sedation, hypothermia and metabolic derangement are excluded.

**Patterns to recognize.**
- Full horizontal movement with doll's eyes but an eye that will not adduct suggests an MLF or CN III lesion.
- Absent responses with intact pupils in a drug overdose: sedatives can suppress the VOR; do not over-read.
- Intact VOR with no voluntary gaze to one side: a supranuclear gaze palsy (for example a frontal eye field lesion) rather than a brainstem nuclear lesion.

**Acute vestibular syndrome.** In a patient with continuous vertigo, nystagmus, nausea and unsteadiness, the HINTS exam (Head Impulse, Nystagmus, Test of Skew) is used. Paradoxically, an abnormal head impulse is reassuring: it localizes to the peripheral nerve. A normal head impulse in a patient with acute continuous vertigo is a red flag for a central lesion such as cerebellar or brainstem stroke. HINTS needs training, applies only to acute continuous vertigo with nystagmus, and does not replace MRI judgment, but in skilled hands it outperforms early diffusion MRI, which can miss small posterior fossa strokes in the first day.

**VOR suppression.** Ask the patient to fix on their thumb at arm's length while rotating head and arm together. Failure to suppress (nystagmus appears) points to cerebellar flocculus dysfunction.

**Rehabilitation.** Vestibular rehabilitation exercises (gaze stabilization with gradually faster head movements) drive cerebellar adaptation and are the mainstay after neuritis or surgery. Prolonged vestibular suppressant medication slows compensation, so it is kept short.

keyPoints: VOR moves the eyes opposite to the head at equal speed to keep images steady
Horizontal arc: horizontal canal → vestibular nucleus → contralateral CN VI → MLF → ipsilateral CN III (medial rectus)
Fast phase of nystagmus names its direction; calorics: COWS (Cold Opposite, Warm Same)
Abnormal head impulse with a catch-up saccade = peripheral loss on the side of the turn
The cerebellar flocculus adapts VOR gain using retinal slip as the error signal

examples.src: Rapid head turn to the left: the eyes are dragged left with the head, then a quick saccade brings them back right to target.
examples.tr: Positive head impulse test: left peripheral vestibular hypofunction (for example left vestibular neuritis).

examples.src: Comatose patient, cold water in the right ear: eyes deviate tonically to the right, no fast phase.
examples.tr: Brainstem VOR intact; the absent fast phase reflects loss of cortical/arousal input.

test.q: When the head turns right, the VOR moves the eyes:
test.explain: The eyes move opposite to the head to keep gaze fixed.

test.q: Ideal VOR gain for a distant target is about:
test.explain: Eye speed matches head speed, so gain ≈ 1.

test.q: Which tract carries the signal from the abducens nucleus to the opposite oculomotor nucleus?
test.explain: Abducens interneurons project through the contralateral MLF to the medial rectus subnucleus.

test.q: Nystagmus is named by the direction of its:
test.explain: By convention, the fast (corrective) phase names the nystagmus.

test.q: Cold water irrigated into the left ear of an awake person causes nystagmus whose fast phase beats:
test.explain: COWS: Cold Opposite. Fast phase to the right.

test.q: A catch-up saccade during a head impulse to the right indicates:
test.explain: The eyes fail to counter-rotate on turns toward the weak (right) side.

test.q: Which structure adapts VOR gain when you get new glasses?
test.explain: The flocculus uses retinal slip to recalibrate gain.

test.q: Before testing doll's eyes in a trauma patient you must:
test.explain: Head rotation risks spinal cord injury if the neck is unstable.

test.q: Why is the VOR better than visual tracking for fast head movement?
choices: Its latency is under about 10 ms
It runs through the visual cortex
It is driven by the optic nerve
test.explain: Very short three-neuron latency beats slow visual feedback.

test.q: In a patient with acute continuous vertigo and nystagmus, a NORMAL head impulse test is concerning for:
choices: Vestibular neuritis of the superior nerve
Impacted ear wax blocking the canal
test.explain: Peripheral neuritis gives an abnormal impulse; a normal one suggests central cause.

test.q: What does the 'V' in VOR stand for?
test.explain: Vestibulo-ocular reflex.

test.q: Caloric mnemonic: Cold Opposite, Warm ___.
test.explain: COWS describes the fast-phase direction.

test.q: What is the bedside name for the oculocephalic reflex? (two words)
test.explain: Turning the head of an unconscious patient tests the VOR.

kidTest.q: When your head turns right, your eyes turn:
kidTest.explain: Eyes go the opposite way to stay on target.

kidTest.q: What helps keep your eyes steady when your head moves?
kidTest.explain: The eye-steadying reflex works automatically.

kidTest.q: Is the reflex fast or slow?
kidTest.explain: It's faster than a blink.

kidTest.q: What happens if you wiggle your thumb fast and keep your head still?
kidTest.explain: Eyes can't track fast thumb movement as well as head movement.

kidTest.q: Which body part tells the eyes the head is moving?
kidTest.explain: The inner ear balance organs drive the reflex.

kidTest.q: Shaking your head while looking at your ___ keeps it clear.
kidTest.explain: The reflex keeps your thumb sharp while your head moves.

advancedTest.q: Climbing fibers carrying retinal slip to the flocculus drive which plasticity during VOR gain learning?
choices: LTP at mossy fiber–granule cell synapses
advancedTest.explain: Marr-Albus-Ito: climbing-fiber error signals induce parallel fiber–Purkinje LTD.

advancedTest.q: Posterior canal BPPV produces nystagmus that is:
advancedTest.explain: Posterior canal links to superior oblique/inferior rectus, giving upbeat-torsional nystagmus.

advancedTest.q: Why does the head impulse remain abnormal after symptoms of vestibular neuritis settle?
choices: Hair cells regrow in the wrong orientation after the infection clears
Central compensation restores static balance but not high-acceleration dynamic responses
The cochlea is damaged, which disturbs the reflex arc for fast turns
Doll's-eye reflexes are suppressed by the cortex after the illness
advancedTest.explain: Ewald's second law: inhibitory cutoff limits compensation for fast turns toward the lesion.

advancedTest.q: A patient can't look left voluntarily, but doll's eyes move both eyes fully left. Lesion?
choices: Left abducens nucleus in the pons
Right abducens nerve in its long course
advancedTest.explain: Intact reflex movement means the brainstem nuclei work; the problem is above them.

lessons.title: Peripheral vs Central Vertigo

levels.kid:
Vertigo is when the room feels like it is spinning, even though you are standing still. It can make you feel sick and wobbly.

Sometimes the problem is in the ear's balance kit. Tiny ear rocks can roll into the wrong loop, or the balance nerve can get a cold. These ear problems feel awful but usually get better.

Other times the problem is in the brain, like a blocked blood vessel in the back of the brain. That is much more serious.

Doctors play detective. They watch how your eyes jiggle, ask if you can walk, and check if your eyes line up. These clues tell them if it's the ear or the brain.
levels.hs:
Vertigo is a false feeling of movement, usually spinning. The key question is where the problem is: **peripheral** (inner ear or vestibular nerve) or **central** (brainstem or cerebellum).

**Common peripheral causes.**
- **BPPV** (benign paroxysmal positional vertigo): loose otoconia drift into a semicircular canal, usually the posterior one. Brief spinning (under a minute) when rolling over in bed or looking up. Treated with a repositioning maneuver (the Epley maneuver).
- **Vestibular neuritis**: inflammation of the vestibular nerve, often after a viral illness. Days of constant vertigo, nausea and unsteadiness, but hearing is normal.
- **Labyrinthitis**: like neuritis but with hearing loss.
- **Ménière disease**: attacks lasting 20 minutes to hours with fluctuating hearing loss, tinnitus and ear fullness.

**Central causes.** Stroke or bleeding in the cerebellum or brainstem, multiple sclerosis, tumors and vestibular migraine.

**Clues for central vertigo.**
- Other neurological signs: double vision, slurred speech, numbness, weakness.
- Severe trouble standing or walking.
- Nystagmus that changes direction with gaze, or is purely vertical.
- Eyes that sit at different heights (skew deviation).

Cerebellar strokes can look like an ear problem, so doctors take sudden vertigo seriously, especially in older people with stroke risk factors.
levels.college:
**Classify by timing and triggers.**
- Episodic, triggered, seconds: BPPV (also orthostatic dizziness, which is not vertigo).
- Episodic, spontaneous, minutes to hours: Ménière disease, vestibular migraine, vertebrobasilar TIA.
- Acute continuous (days): vestibular neuritis or labyrinthitis vs posterior circulation stroke.
- Chronic: bilateral vestibulopathy, cerebellar degeneration, persistent postural-perceptual dizziness (PPPD).

**Nystagmus in peripheral lesions.** Unidirectional, horizontal with a torsional component, beating away from the lesioned side, increased by gaze in the fast-phase direction (Alexander's law), and suppressed by visual fixation.

**Nystagmus in central lesions.** Direction-changing with gaze, pure vertical (downbeat suggests a cervicomedullary or flocculus lesion; upbeat suggests brainstem/medullary), pure torsional, and often not suppressed by fixation.

**HINTS.** In acute continuous vertigo with nystagmus, any of these suggests central cause ("INFARCT"): Impulse Normal, Fast-phase Alternating, Refixation on Cover Test (skew). HINTS plus new hearing loss ("HINTS plus") raises concern for AICA infarction.

**BPPV specifics.** Posterior canal BPPV: Dix-Hallpike provokes upbeating, torsional nystagmus (top pole toward the down ear) after a short latency, lasting under a minute, fatiguing with repeats. Treat with the Epley maneuver. Horizontal canal BPPV: supine roll test gives geotropic or apogeotropic horizontal nystagmus; treat with a barbecue roll or Gufoni maneuver.

**Lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome.** Vertebral or PICA occlusion: vertigo, nystagmus, ipsilateral facial pain/temperature loss, contralateral body pain/temperature loss, ipsilateral Horner syndrome, dysphagia and hoarseness (nucleus ambiguus), and ipsilateral limb ataxia.

**Imaging.** CT is poor for posterior fossa ischemia. MRI with diffusion is preferred but can be falsely negative early in small brainstem strokes.
levels.phd:
**Why peripheral nystagmus is horizontal-torsional.** Vestibular neuritis usually affects the superior vestibular nerve (innervating the horizontal and anterior canals plus utricle), likely because its bony canal is longer and narrower. Loss of tonic input from those canals creates an imbalance in the vestibular nuclei whose vector sum is a horizontal-torsional slow phase toward the lesion. Inferior nerve sparing explains why posterior canal BPPV can later occur in the same ear. Isolated inferior neuritis is rarer and harder to detect with standard calorics, which test only the horizontal canal.

**Skew deviation and the ocular tilt reaction.** Utricular graviceptive pathways cross in the pons and ascend in the MLF to the interstitial nucleus of Cajal. Imbalance yields the ocular tilt reaction: head tilt, ocular torsion and skew deviation. Lesions below the crossing tilt toward the lesion; above, away. Peripheral utricular loss can cause a small skew, but a clear vertical misalignment favors a central lesion.

**Ménière pathophysiology.** Endolymphatic hydrops (distension of the endolymphatic space) is the histological hallmark, now visualized with delayed gadolinium MRI. Hydrops is not identical to disease, since asymptomatic hydrops exists, so mechanisms likely include ionic disturbance from membrane microruptures and dysregulated endolymph homeostasis.

**Vestibular migraine** is common and diagnosed by recurrent vestibular episodes with migraine history and migrainous features in at least half the episodes. Interictal central eye signs occur in some patients. Mechanisms likely involve trigeminovascular input to the vestibular nuclei and altered thalamocortical multisensory processing.

**PPPD** reflects maladaptive plasticity after an acute vestibular event: persistent reliance on visual cues and stiffened postural control, with increased activity in visual-vestibular areas and reduced connectivity in vestibular cortex, illustrating functional (not structural) disease.

**Diagnostic accuracy.** Studies of HINTS by trained examiners report high sensitivity for stroke, exceeding early MRI-DWI, but sensitivity drops when applied broadly by untrained clinicians to patients without continuous vertigo and nystagmus, highlighting spectrum bias.
levels.expert:
**Triage mindset.** About a quarter of patients with isolated acute vertigo and stroke risk factors who have a central cause will present without obvious focal deficits. The danger is the cerebellar infarct labeled "inner ear" and sent home, then swelling compresses the fourth ventricle and brainstem.

**Red flags.** New headache or neck pain (vertebral dissection), inability to sit or stand unaided (truncal ataxia from vermis involvement), any focal deficit, vertical or direction-changing nystagmus, skew, a normal head impulse in acute continuous vertigo, and new unilateral hearing loss with vertigo.

**Neurosurgical emergency: cerebellar infarct or hemorrhage.** Large cerebellar infarcts swell over 2-4 days. Watch for falling consciousness, new gaze palsy, bilateral signs and obstructive hydrocephalus. Management can include an external ventricular drain, but suboccipital decompressive craniectomy, often with resection of infarcted tissue, is the definitive life-saving step; guidelines support it for deterioration due to brainstem compression. A drain alone risks upward herniation. Cerebellar hemorrhage over about 3 cm, or with brainstem compression or hydrocephalus, generally warrants surgical evacuation.

**Management of peripheral causes.**
- BPPV: Epley (posterior canal) has strong evidence; avoid unnecessary imaging and long-term vestibular suppressants.
- Vestibular neuritis: short symptomatic treatment, early vestibular rehabilitation; corticosteroids remain debated.
- Ménière disease: lifestyle measures and diuretics are traditional; intratympanic steroids, then intratympanic gentamicin (chemical labyrinthectomy) for refractory vertigo; surgical labyrinthectomy or vestibular nerve section are last resorts.

**Mimics.** Presyncope from arrhythmia, hypoglycemia and medication side effects are often called dizziness. Vertebrobasilar TIA can produce isolated episodic vertigo before a basilar stroke: recurrent brief spontaneous vertigo in a vascular patient deserves vascular imaging, not reassurance.

keyPoints: Peripheral: BPPV, vestibular neuritis, labyrinthitis, Ménière disease; central: posterior circulation stroke, MS, tumors, vestibular migraine
Peripheral nystagmus is unidirectional horizontal-torsional and suppressed by fixation
Central signs: direction-changing or vertical nystagmus, skew, normal head impulse, severe ataxia, focal deficits
HINTS (Head Impulse, Nystagmus, Test of Skew) separates peripheral from central in acute continuous vertigo
BPPV: brief positional vertigo, Dix-Hallpike to diagnose, Epley maneuver to treat
Swelling cerebellar infarcts may need suboccipital decompression

examples.tr: Right posterior canal BPPV; treat with a right Epley maneuver.

examples.src: Sudden vertigo, cannot walk unaided, direction-changing nystagmus, normal head impulse.
examples.tr: Central pattern: suspect cerebellar stroke and image with MRI.

test.q: Brief spinning lasting seconds when rolling over in bed suggests:
test.explain: Positional, brief, recurrent vertigo is classic BPPV.

test.q: BPPV most commonly involves which canal?
test.explain: Gravity makes otoconia settle in the posterior canal most often.

test.q: Days of constant vertigo after a cold, with normal hearing and no other neurological signs, most suggests:
test.explain: Neuritis spares hearing; labyrinthitis includes hearing loss.

test.q: Episodes of vertigo lasting hours with fluctuating hearing loss, tinnitus and ear fullness:
test.explain: Ménière's triad plus episodic vertigo.

test.q: Which nystagmus suggests a CENTRAL cause?
choices: Nystagmus beating away from the bad ear
test.explain: Pure vertical nystagmus localizes centrally.

test.q: In HINTS, which head impulse result is reassuring for a peripheral cause in acute continuous vertigo?
choices: Head impulse is not part of HINTS
test.explain: An abnormal impulse localizes to the nerve; normal is worrying.

test.q: Vertical misalignment of the eyes on cover testing is called:
test.explain: Skew deviation is a central sign in HINTS.

test.q: The best imaging test for suspected posterior fossa stroke is:
test.explain: CT misses many posterior fossa infarcts.

test.q: Wallenberg (lateral medullary) syndrome usually involves occlusion of the:
test.explain: Lateral medulla is supplied by vertebral/PICA branches.

test.q: Which feature is a red flag in acute vertigo?
choices: Inability to stand or walk unaided
test.explain: Severe truncal ataxia suggests cerebellar involvement.

test.q: Name the repositioning maneuver for posterior canal BPPV.
test.explain: The Epley maneuver moves otoconia back into the utricle.

test.q: The diagnostic test for posterior canal BPPV is the Dix-___ maneuver.
test.explain: Dix-Hallpike provokes positional nystagmus.

test.q: What does the 'S' in HINTS stand for? (Test of ___)
test.explain: Head Impulse, Nystagmus, Test of Skew.

kidTest.q: What does vertigo feel like?
kidTest.explain: Vertigo is a false spinning feeling.

kidTest.q: Ear rocks rolling into the wrong loop can cause:
choices: Spinning when you move your head
A broken arm from falling over
A bad tooth ache in your mouth
kidTest.explain: That's BPPV, a common ear cause.

kidTest.q: Which is more serious?
choices: Ear rocks in the wrong place
A blocked blood vessel in the brain
kidTest.explain: Brain problems like strokes are emergencies.

kidTest.q: What do doctors watch to find the cause?
kidTest.explain: Eye movements give strong clues.

kidTest.q: Do most ear causes of vertigo get better?
kidTest.explain: Most ear problems improve.

kidTest.q: Feeling like the room spins is called ___.
kidTest.explain: Vertigo means a false sense of movement.

advancedTest.q: Why can a patient develop posterior canal BPPV after superior vestibular neuritis?
choices: Neuritis makes new otoconia in the cochlea that drift into the canals
Steroid treatment loosens otoconia from the utricle into the canals
The posterior canal is innervated by the spared inferior vestibular nerve
Neuritis spreads to the inferior nerve and irritates the canal directly
advancedTest.explain: The inferior division often survives, so the posterior canal still functions and can be stimulated by debris.

advancedTest.q: A large cerebellar infarct with falling consciousness and fourth-ventricle compression is best managed by:
choices: Observation with repeat CT in a day
Lumbar puncture to lower the pressure
advancedTest.explain: Decompression treats brainstem compression; LP is dangerous with posterior fossa mass effect.

advancedTest.q: Ocular tilt reaction from a lesion ABOVE the pontine crossing of utricular pathways tilts the head:
advancedTest.explain: Below the decussation: ipsilesional tilt; above: contralesional.

advancedTest.q: HINTS sensitivity falls when used broadly mainly because:
choices: MRI performs better than HINTS even when used by trained examiners
HINTS has poor validation in acute vestibular syndrome cohorts
Skew deviation is a peripheral sign, so it misleads examiners toward central causes
It is applied to patients without acute continuous vertigo and nystagmus, and by untrained examiners
advancedTest.explain: Spectrum bias and examiner skill reduce accuracy outside its validated population.
